en: [0] Success! Homage to the Three Jewels.

[1.1] Now the Blessed One was dwelling in the great city of Vārāṇasī; he taught the Dharma to sentient beings by performing great benefit for them—namely, that which brings about the fulfillment of all hopes and desires and accomplishes what is auspicious. This was amidst a great assembly of followers, including the retinue of the Naga kings headed by Takṣaka, and a great assembly of gods and humans.

[1.2] Now, in the city of Navanagara, there was a brahmin named Viṣṇudatta, wealthy, possessing great riches and vast enjoyments, endowed with abundant wealth and resources, and one who had mastered the Vedas and the Vedāṅgas. He was a practitioner of mantras and an achiever of mantra-siddhi. He repeatedly invoked the nāgas and performed the *agnihotra* sacrifice. At the time of the harvest, that brahmin encountered a severe drought. Then, by means of the sound of his self-assertion (*ahaṃkāra*) and in accordance with the words of the mantra, he spoke thus: "O showers of rain—"

"I shall release them; I will summon the nāgas. With that, he prepared the *agnihotra* sacrifice and offered oblations of sesame, rice, mustard seeds, and pungent oil. He fashioned an image representing a certain malevolent nāga. Having consecrated an iron stake with mantras, he drove it into the head of that nāga. That nāga’s head split open, and he experienced intense agony. Thereupon, that nāga became even more enraged with great fury. Then—

In an instant, a moment, or a brief hour, his own body—possessing the speed of a serpent’s glide and accompanied by great pain—was released. Then those rays emitted from his body burned the fields of that brahmin; having covered them with great torment, a massive shower of fire was cast down upon the brahmin’s body. And that brahmin, abandoning his *agnihotra* sacrifices, was without protection, without refuge, and without resort; there was no one at all to save him.

Seeking the Blessed One as his refuge, protection, and final resort, he began to cry out in distress. He ran toward the Blessed One; having approached where the Blessed One was, he prostrated at the Blessed One’s feet and said: "May the Blessed One protect me! May the Sugata protect me! A fierce elephant is intent on destroying my life, and there is no one to save me."

[1.3] Then the Blessed One, having comforted that great brahmin, spoke thus: "Do not be afraid, O great brahmin; I shall be your refuge, your resort, and your ultimate protection. [The brahmin] remained silent.

[1.4] Then indeed, Vajrapāṇi, the great yakṣa general, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Behold, Blessed One, how by the wicked nāga, through his manifest presence, all the crops have been destroyed. Therefore, after you have passed into nirvāṇa, at a future time and in a future age, what will be the refuge for all sentient beings? May the Blessed One therefore speak concerning the protection of the crops, the warding off of the nāgas, and for the sake of all the crops; so that all the crops shall be restored, well-guarded, and made to flourish."

[1.5] Then the Blessed One said this to Vajrapāṇi, the Lord of the Guhyakas: "Vajrapāṇi, there exists a dhāraṇī called the *Vajra-Subduer of Nāgas*, which is the heart-mantra and seal of the Tathāgatas, spoken by former Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Perfectly Enlightened Ones. I too shall now speak it, by means of which there will be the protection of all crops for the sake of quickly averting affliction; they shall be well-guarded."

It shall serve as a boundary-binding for all *nāgas*. Great mountain precipices of fire, and masses of clouds of great flames of fire from all four directions, manifesting the speed of the *garuḍa* bird, shall cover the sky; this chapter remains for the protection of all flowers and fruits, by which all *nāgas* and others will be set ablaze, and all wicked *nāgas* will perish.
[1.6] Then Vajrapāṇi, the great general of the yakṣas, said this to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One teach the words of the great dhāraṇī-mantra; act for the benefit of all sentient beings!
[1.7] Then the Blessed One spoke this heart-essence (hṛdaya):

Homage to the Blessed Buddhas! Homage to the Blessed King Śākyamuni! Oṃ, blaze, blaze! O you who dwell in the mountain, you of blazing speed, you who strike the heart of the Great Fierce One! Huru huru! Strike, strike! Burn, burn! Cook, cook! Cause all to be cooked! [Destroy] the lineage and clan of the nāgas that destroy all crops! Hold, hold! O you of preeminent fierce speed, great power and prowess, you whose face is throbbing and terrible!

Matha matha! O you who bear garlands of flames, O you of fierce speed, O bearer of the excellent celestial chariot, *hūṃ hūṃ*! O powerful one, O swift one, disperse, disperse! You who sustain all crops, grasses, shrubs, medicinal herbs, forest trees, flowers, fruits, and leaves! May all the evils of the *nāgas* depart! O you whose speed has left all abodes, *svāhā*! *Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*! O rending of the *nāgas*, *phaṭ*! O garlanded with flames, *phaṭ svāhā*!

[1.8] As soon as this vidyā was spoken by the Blessed One, it became the destroyer of all nāgas and all evil afflictions. All the great nāgas were afflicted with diseases of the head; their bodies became moist, foul-smelling, and putrid. At the feet of the Blessed One...

Having prostrated themselves, they spoke thus: "O Blessed One, extremely terrible mantra-words have been spoken. O Blessed One, know that this is my transgression; however, O Blessed One, I am treated with contempt by a wicked vidyādhara. He strikes me and casts me out. Then, O Blessed One, the wicked nāgas are agitated; then they destroy the crops, they destroy the flowers and fruits, they let fall thunderbolts, and [send forth] cold winds."

They cause agitation; they bring down excessive rain, drought, and unseasonable rain. However, Blessed One, a practitioner of mantras who possesses the knowledge-mantra (*vidyādhara*) must abide in loving-kindness (*maitrī*). He must be armored with the being of loving-kindness; he must hold the sword of loving-kindness in his hand. By means of loving-kindness, all malevolent beings are subdued. Furthermore, Blessed One, from this day forward, I shall make a vow in the presence of the Tathāgata.

"O Blessed One, wherever this king of the Vidyādharas shall move about, there we Nāgas will no longer cause harm. Wherever this Heart Dhāraṇī has been employed for protection—where it provides rescue, support, preservation, the binding of boundaries, and the binding of the maṇḍala—and where the Pratisarā has been employed, O Blessed One, we shall constantly and perpetually ward off all calamities for that person."

[1.9] Then the Blessed One gave his approval to those lords of the nāgas: "Excellent, excellent, O lords of the serpents! You must act in this way; with yourselves well-protected, Jambudvīpa must be protected by you."

[1.10] Now, therefore, I shall explain the procedure for the ritual service (*upacāra*), which is auspicious and effectuates all rites. When the crops are being crushed [by pests], they become agitated. At that time, the *vidyādhara* should construct a square mandala in the middle of a field or in a forest. Four full vases should be placed there. It should be strewn with flowers. Seven circles of coins (*rūpaka*) should be made, as well as a circle of rice (*taṇḍula*).

One should prepare twenty-one individual forms. One should set out food, milk-rice (*pāyasa*), rice mixed with sesame (*kṛsara*), curd, and milk. Fruits and flowers should be placed there. Four water-jars (*ghaṭikā*) should be set out. A great offering (*mahābali*) beginning with roasted barley flour (*saktu*) should be placed in front. In the center of the mandala, a sacrificial pit (*kuṇḍa*) should be established; it should be filled with the five products of the cow (*pañcagavya*), milk, and water. Mustard seeds and parched grain (*lāja*) should be scattered [into it].

The mantra should be recited sixty times over four stakes made of acacia wood (*khadira*) and fashioned from iron. Each stake should be eight finger-breadths (*aṅgula*) in length. In the four corners of the mandala, four serpents (*nāga*) should be fashioned using the dung of a tawny cow (*kapila*). An acacia stake should be driven into the heart of each serpent so that it is entirely buried. One hundred and eight times the mantra should be recited. To the east, a seven-headed serpent should be established.

In the western direction, one with eight heads; in the southern, one with five heads; in the northern, one with three heads; and in the center of the mandala, a nine-headed nāga should be placed. Four incense burners should be set out, with the fifth in the central mandala. Having recited this dhāraṇī twenty-one times over parched grain mixed with mustard seeds, they should be scattered in the four directions. This dhāraṇī, having been written down, should be fastened to the tops of banners at the four corners of the mandala.

They should be placed in the middle of a field, and they should be placed in the middle of a grove. By the mere act of placing them, a boundary-binding of great mountain precipices is established all around in the four directions.

[1.11] As long as the ritual peg (kīlaka) is not extracted, so long does the binding of the great boundary (mahāsīmābandha) remain. All crops, all flowers, and all fruits will be well-protected; even a single leaf shall not wither, let alone the tips of the branches. All species of living beings—beasts and birds alike—will have their mouths bound; they will be unable to cause destruction. Even those who have perished shall regain their vitality once more;
they shall again approach with strength, nourishment, and vigor. And that vessel (kuṇḍa)—

The fields and groves in all four directions should be sprinkled. All living beings will perish; snakes, mice, mongooses, porcupines, hairy frogs, gadflies, mosquitoes, locusts, and flocks of birds will perish; all worms will perish; even down to the smallest insects, none shall remain. It is never possible to prevent their destruction.

As long as this stake is not pulled out, there shall be no emergence of creatures born from moisture, those born spontaneously, or even those born from eggs, nor shall species of living beings produced from stone-flowers arise; nor shall various Naga-afflictions prevail again. As long as the stake is not pulled out, all crops, flowers, and fruits will ripen in peace and abundance; they will become delicious and soft. All Nagas will constantly and perpetually provide protection, defense, and guardianship.

[1.12] Having recited the mantra over sand twenty-one times, it should be scattered upon all trees—those with grain, flowers, fruit, and leaves. All living beings will fall and perish; all snails, *trailāṭakas*, venomous serpents, centipedes, and various other species of living creatures will perish. As long as the stake is not pulled out, they shall not exist.

[1.13] In four locations, the rite for the pacification of the field (*kṣetra-śāntika*) should be performed. One should offer oblations of barley, sesame, mustard seeds, and rice smeared with ghee; there will be great peace (*mahāśānti*). Even that which belongs to the animal realm cannot be destroyed. This is the *dhāraṇī*.

It should be drawn according to the complete ritual procedure for offerings. Having depicted the Blessed Buddha, the sage Agastya, and Vajradhara, they should be placed upon the tip of a banner in a high location. Offerings of food, flowers, and incense should be presented. A wooden stake made of *khadira* wood, measuring eight finger-breadths in length, should be driven into the top of the arrow-shaft one thousand times; thus all winds, cold, clouds, and thunderbolts will be paralyzed.

It shall come to pass: the creatures that destroy all crops, flowers, fruits, and leaves will perish. All species of living beings—such as gadflies, mosquitoes, ants, locusts, flies, *sphurama*-flies, bees, worms, *śṛṅgalikā*-creatures, *vātālika*-insects, owls, mice, long-faced creatures, and so forth—will all perish; they will no longer exist. They will all go to destruction. Crows, ravens, sparrows, *cañcaṭika*-birds, pigeons, *surika*-birds, owls, wagtails, parrots, mynas, and the like—all will perish.
[1.14] This mantra for the ritual peg that binds the directions (*diśābandhakīlaka*) should be recited:
*namo buddhasya | ili mili caṇḍo micili caṇḍa caṇḍa caṇḍe bandhaya svāhā*.

[1.15] Then the great seer Agastya, seated not far from the Blessed One, having heard this dhāraṇī, rose from his seat, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One as follows: "O Blessed One, I shall bind the mouths, restrain, and threaten all species of living beings—whether wicked or extremely malevolent, whether venomous, or those that destroy crops, flowers, fruits, leaves, stalks, and roots. I shall establish a boundary extending for a great league in every direction throughout the four quarters."

"I shall protect it. Blessed One, in the future time, in the final age, I shall ward off all the wicked and most malevolent ones. I shall bestow these mantra-words upon you. Therefore, Blessed One, for the sake of the welfare and benefit of all sentient beings, and for the purpose of protecting crops, flowers, fruits, and leaves.
Then that great ṛṣi, standing before the Blessed One, spoke this dhāraṇī.

Homage to the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata. Homage to Agastya, the great ṛṣi. It is as follows: *kṛmi*, *cūri*, *cameli*, *vara vara*, *he vila*, *bandhani nāśani*, *daha daha*, *sumuri*, *cari*. O binder of all the wicked, binder of the mouth, you who encompass all! *kṣa kṣa kṣa*, *maṇi*, *kṣariṣi vasari*, *phuli phuṭi phuṭi samariṭi*. May all beings of sinful nature depart! *kṣadhili svāhā*.

[1.17] Immediately after this spell was spoken by the great seer Agasti in the presence of the Blessed One, all those wicked nāgas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas fell with their faces downward. They cried out to the Blessed One in a loud voice: "We are ruined, O Blessed One! We have been cursed by the seer's curse; we are burned, O Blessed One! We have been utterly consumed by the fire of the seer's curse. O Blessed One, we shall no longer harass the beings in Jambudvīpa."
"And furthermore, Blessed One, we shall no longer destroy the crops, leaves, flowers, and fruits; we shall ward them off from every living creature.

Then the Blessed One said: "O Lord of Nagas, you must act in this way. You must protect all beings in Jambudvīpa; thus we shall become those who cause the increase of all crops, leaves, flowers, fruits, foliage, and happiness."

[1.19] Then that Great Sage will explain the ritual procedure for the offering: "O Blessed One, this vidyā is the heart of the Great Sage. Having recited it one hundred and eight times over a water vessel, one should stand facing the east and cast it in the four directions while observing the sage’s silence: *ara sara śara pāśa sapta-ṛṣi-hṛdaya-krodhāt ca mukhaṃ bandhaya prāṇavara ghumuru cale svāhā*."

In this manner, it should be recited seven times. Merely by its application, all wicked *nāgas* become scorched; all species of living beings, from bipeds to quadrupeds, become tormented by the curse and all depart. No further harm shall afflict the crops in that region, and all species of living beings shall perish [from that place]. Furthermore, flowers, fruits, leaves, and crops shall no longer be destroyed.

[1.20] Then the Blessed One gave his approval to that great ṛṣi, saying: "Excellent, excellent, great ṛṣi! It is right for you to act in such a way that all sentient beings will be well-protected, and all crops, flowers, and fruits will be well-protected.
[1.21] Then Vajrapāṇi, the great general of the yakṣas, said this to the Blessed One: "May the Blessed One empower me; in the future time, in the final age, I shall guard and protect [this teaching].
[1.22] "Excellent, excellent, Vajrapāṇi! Protect all sentient beings."
[1.23] The Ritual for the Affliction of Crops belonging to the *Nāgahṛdaya* is completed.

[2.1] Then the Blessed One, with a great retinue, a great assembly, a great array, through the power of his great supernatural might, and by manifesting a great miracle, went to the palace of the Great King Vaiśravaṇa.

[2.2] Then the Blessed One arrived not far from the abode of Vaiśravaṇa. In that region of the earth was a choice forest grove named Viṣavaka. In the midst of that forest grove there was a lotus pond. By the power of that lotus pond, the fields, parks, forests, and groves in the capital city of Aḍakavatī were filled with flowers and fruits; as were all the men, women, boys, and girls, along with the cattle, horses, mares, buffaloes, elephants, camels, donkeys, and other animals.

They became thoroughly satiated with happiness. And that lotus pond was two *yojanas* in width, extending for four *vyāmas* on all four sides. That lotus pond was covered with various kinds of blue, red, white, and yellow lotuses; it contained various forms such as fish, crocodiles, *timiṅgila* fish, porpoises, bees, and various aquatic creatures. [2.3] Then, at a time when no rain had fallen, all the flowers, fruits, leaves, and foliage of the forest were withered, and those flowers faded away. Consequently, the fish, crocodiles, *timiṅgila* fish, porpoises, bees, and various aquatic creatures were deprived of water.
When only a small amount of water remained, they ran and rushed about in the ten directions; with hearts afflicted by the threat to their lives and the destruction of their existence, they fled.

Then the Blessed One arrived at the vicinity of that lotus pond. Accompanied by a great retinue, he saw there many hundreds of thousands of fish, makaras, porpoises, and dolphins running toward the ten directions to preserve their lives, looking on piteously. The Blessed One, having comforted them, let out the sound of snapping his fingers as a basis for loving-kindness (*maitryālambana*), calling to the nāgas a second and a third time.

When a snap of the fingers is made, its sound is heard throughout the triple-thousand great thousandfold world system. Due to certain prior karmic conditions, there is an obstruction to the life-force of those beings; because of that, the great nāgas do not hear the sound, nor do they recollect the Blessed One.

[2.5] Then the yakṣa general of Māra’s host named Vairambhaka, raising his voice and proclaiming it throughout the triple-thousand great-thousandfold world system, cried out: "Great terrors arise in the world! On the seventh day, the conflagration at the end of the aeon will break forth. There shall be nothing that is not consumed by fire, from the Peak of Existence down to the Avīci hell. [2.6] Then all those gods, nāgas, yakṣas, gandharvas, asuras, garuḍas, kinnaras, mahoragas, humans, and non-humans...
Having heard this sound, they cried out, "Alas! Alas! What a tragedy! What a great calamity! Destructive forces have arisen in the world!

[2.7] Then the Blessed One, knowing that this was experienced as a result of karma, thought, "I must pay attention to this. Thereupon, the Blessed One emitted a ray of light from the circle of hair between his brows (*ūrṇākośa*). Those rays illuminated all the abodes of the nāgas; having illuminated them, they returned once more and vanished into the *uṣṇīṣa* on the crown of his head.

[2.8] Then the Naga king Samantākāracchatracandrākaraparikara, having assembled all the nagas, said this to them: "O nagas, what is the reason for the appearance of these rays? By what cause have they arisen in the world?
[2.9] Then the Naga king Sāgara, reflecting, realized that these rays had been manifested through the power of the Blessed One.

[2.10] Then Sāgara, the Nāga king, together with other Nāga kings of great supernatural power, approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and said this: "Blessed One, for what cause does the emission of rays proceed? What is the reason? By means of the emission of rays, all the abodes were illuminated, and then they returned once more. [2.11] The Blessed One spoke thus: "O Lord of Serpents, many hundreds of thousands of living beings are being deprived of their lives."
[2.12] Then, in that very instant, moment, and second, Sāgara, the great nāga king, filled the lotus pond with torrents of rain and caused it to overflow.

[2.13] Then, a vast open space appeared in that region of the earth. There, in that region of the earth, the Blessed One sat down, surrounded and honored in the midst of a great assembly, encompassed by a great host of nāgas—namely, eighty thousand great nāga kings who had gathered there, headed by the nāga king Sāgara.

[2.14] Then the great Naga king Samantākāracchatrākāraparikara rose from his seat, draped his upper robe over one shoulder, and placed his right knee upon the ground. Approaching the Blessed One, he bowed his head at the Blessed One’s feet, circumambulated him three times, and honored the Blessed One with various flowers, perfumes, garlands, ointments, ornaments, and garments. Having offered these honors, he sat down before him.

[2.15] Then the four Great Kings, having bowed with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was, addressed the Blessed One as follows: “Blessed One, most terrible and great fears have arisen in the world, namely: drought, famine, and wildernesses. Because of this calamity, Blessed One, all sentient beings have become without protection and without refuge.
May the Blessed One speak such mantra-words so that, in the future time, in the final age, the world may be delivered from the convergence of various calamities.”

For the purpose of destroying excessive rain, drought, thunderbolts, cold, and heat; for the purpose of pacifying famine and wildernesses; for the purpose of warding off [calamities]; and for the purpose of protection—please recite the *dhāraṇī* mantra words.

[2.16] Then the Blessed One spoke thus to the great king Vaiśravaṇa, the great king Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the great king Virūḍhaka, and the great king Virūpākṣa: "Great kings, there exists a dhāraṇī of mantra-words called *Samantajvalitavidyun*, the Heart of Exhortation, by the mere hearing of which all the abodes of the nāgas and all the bodies of the nāgas will burst into flames, and the hearts of all wicked nāgas will be agitated."

The heads of all the nāgas will split into seven pieces; their eyes and crowns will burst open and fall apart into fragments. O Great Kings, seize them for the sake of destroying the wicked and the extremely malevolent, and for the sake of protecting all sentient beings. Then the Four Great Kings prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and spoke thus: "Blessed One, please speak the mantra words of the dhāraṇī called *Samantajvalitavidyun*, the inciting heart-mantra of the nāgas."

[2.18] Then the Blessed One, having gazed with the gaze of a nāga—the gaze of all Tathāgatas—having assembled the entire assembly of nāgas, spoke thus: "Listen, O lords of serpents, to these mantra-words of the dhāraṇī."

It is as follows: Oṃ vipulapravare! O Nāga, Mahānāga, you who revolve the heart of the Nāgas! Blaze, blaze, [consuming] the hearts of all Nāgas! Kimi kimi! O destroyer of the Nāga clans! Strike, strike the hearts of all wicked Nāgas! Burn, burn all the abodes of the Nāgas! Cook, cook, cause to be cooked, cause to be cooked all the wicked Nāgas! Tread upon, tread upon [all those with] the stainless stride of the oceans and seas, O supreme one with the majesty of the Great Nāga! Svāhā!

[2.19] As soon as the Blessed One had uttered these mantra-words of the *Nāgahṛdayadhāraṇī*, all those nāgas began to tremble violently; their bodies became withered, moist, and foul-smelling, as if they were being consumed by flames. Burning as if by a fire, they cried out in loud voices to the Blessed One in great distress and said this to him: "Blessed One, extremely terrible mantra-words have been spoken! They are afflicting our very hearts."

"O Blessed One, we are ruined; we are being consumed by fire! From this day forward, O Blessed One, out of a sense of collective responsibility, we shall make a vow before the Blessed One: we shall protect all leaves, flowers, fruits, foliage, and crops; we shall release showers of rain at the proper times; we shall bring about happiness and gladness; and we shall cause all crops, flowers, and fruits to flourish in accordance with the words of the Tathāgata."

We shall protect [it]; we shall establish it through our vow of truth. We shall protect all sentient beings like an only son. O Blessed One, wherever on this earth this King of Vidyādharas shall circulate, there, O Blessed One, we shall dwell with every form of provision. O Blessed One, by mere recollection, we—all of us—constantly release showers of rain; by mere recollection, we also ward off excessive rain.
"And we shall not violate what is authorized by the words of the Tathāgata. Furthermore, Blessed One, we shall provide the mantra-words of the *śapathadhāraṇī*.
Then all those nāga kings, having prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, spoke thus:
Namely: Oṃ caṭa caṭa vicaṭa vicaṭa śletha śletha śavari ciṭi svāhā."

“O Blessed One, may we not become foul-smelling, nor may we fail to become perfectly enlightened ones (samyaksaṃbuddhas), nor may there be for us a fall from the womb of a nāga. O Blessed One, if on that very night and day, by means of the ritual procedure performed by the vidyādhara, we do not release showers of rain throughout all of Jambudvīpa for the sake of protecting all sentient beings, then, O Blessed One, this vidyādhara must recollect these words of the dhāraṇī-mantra—the words of the oath—seven times, while first recalling the previous mantra.”

Then, O Blessed One, one should offer the *caṇḍabīja* [mantra] one hundred and eight times into the fire of the *nāga*. At that time, O Blessed One, all our abodes will be set ablaze by the flames of fire; our bodies will be shattered into pieces until only a skeleton remains. Then, O Blessed One, we shall all swiftly release torrents of rain. If you do not swiftly release the torrents of rain, then, O Blessed One, everyone will fall under the power of death;
we shall die along with our sons and grandsons.

[2.21] Then the four great kings, headed by Vaiśravaṇa, said this to the Blessed One: “Blessed One, these words of the dragon’s curse-mantra are exceedingly terrible; they are words of a curse spoken without compassion.”

The Blessed One said: "In the future time, in the final age, there will be great kings who are wicked, fierce, violent, reckless, and harmful toward the *nāgas*. Therefore, by means of this oath, they become afraid and terrified; they release showers of rain from time to time, and they shall produce crops, flowers, and fruits from time to time.
Then the Great King Vaiśravaṇa said this to the Blessed One: "Speak, Blessed One, the detailed procedure for the ritual service (*upacāra*)."

[2.24] Then the Blessed One spoke the ritual procedure for the preparatory service: "In a time overwhelmed by drought, one should prepare a mandala on a mountain, in a forest hermitage, or in a monastery; or at a spring, a lake, a pond, a well, a river, or in the abode of a nāga. It should be made with clay and cow dung measuring three cubits. In the center of the mandala, one should dig a pit one cubit deep and four-cornered, measuring one cubit."

It should be made very smooth and well-swept; it should be sprinkled all around with scented water. In the center of that excavation, four nāga kings should be fashioned from cow dung and earth mixed with brownish-yellow [pigment], having nine heads in the form of hoods.

The body is to be depicted in a crouched posture. A *cintāmaṇi* jewel is to be placed upon the head in every instance. In the eastern direction, Sāgara, the king of nāgas, is to be depicted. In the southern direction, Mahānāgarāja, surrounded by a retinue of parasols of various forms, is to be depicted. In the western direction, Varuṇa, the king of nāgas, is to be depicted. In the northern direction, Lambūlaka, the king of nāgas, is to be depicted. Each is to be accompanied by a retinue of seven.

The bodies should be anointed with various perfumes—whether they have three heads, two heads, or five heads. Having ground sandalwood, red sandalwood, fragrant sandalwood, *padmaka*, and saffron, one should sprinkle them with incense powders. Flower garlands should be offered. Popped rice and mustard seeds should be scattered there within the palace. And in the four directions, it should be strewn with flowers.

The four Great Kings should be installed in the corners. In the four directions, images of the Buddhas containing relics and reliquaries containing relics should be installed. It should be adorned with silk banners and flags. Offerings should be made. One should burn aloeswood, sandalwood, turuṣka, tagara, nalada, kunduruka, medaka, parched grain, mustard seeds, and resin, mixing them with honey. Having recited the mantra twenty-one times, this incense should be offered to the nāgas.

Around the entire perimeter of the outer mandala, it should be decorated with barley-flour lotuses. Having divided [the area] into four gates, seven offerings filled with oblations should be placed on each side. One should place a white offering consisting of various kinds of flavors as they are available, and it should be strewn with flowers. It should be arranged with various offerings; it should be strewn with fruits. Four full jars should be set out, and four pots filled with oblations should be stationed.

While burning guggulu incense in four incense burners, eight lamps should be lit. The Vidyādhara should offer oblations at the eastern gate; he should offer one hundred and eight oblations of karavīra wood mixed with mustard seeds and rock salt. When the one hundred and eighth oblation is completed, all the nāgas release torrents of rain; they release torrents of rain everywhere throughout Jambudvīpa in the four directions. All become eager, and all the nāgas rejoice. This is the first procedure.

[2.25] One should prepare pills from the powder of mustard seeds, pungent oil, madhuka, karavīra flowers, and nāgapuṣpa flowers. Then these pills should be cast into a lake inhabited by nāgas. As soon as they are cast in, accompanied by the recitation of the mantra one hundred and eight times, all the nāgas rejoice; they release great torrents of rain. If it does not rain immediately, the bodies of those nāgas will fall apart; they will suffer from headaches, and painful afflictions will arise. This is the second procedure.

[2.26] Having taken the ashes of the oblation and stirred them with sour gruel (*kāñjika*), one should recite the mantra over them sixty times. They should be thrown into the middle of the house. As soon as they are thrown, all the *nāgas* become overwhelmed; then they release torrents of rain. If it does not rain immediately, the bodies of all those *nāgas* will become afflicted with leprosy (*citra-kuṣṭha*).
This is the third procedure.

[2.27] A wise person, having infused lotus, sunflower, blue lotus, yellow orpiment, mixed copper powder, mustard seeds, *indravāruṇī*, and *palāśa* with molasses juice, should fashion pills. Having consecrated them eighty times with the mantra, pills the size of jujube fruits should be made. Seven pills should be cast into the abode of the Nāgas; during a time of drought, they will cause rain to fall continuously within seven days and nights.

If it does not rain immediately, then everything in the abode of the nāgas will wither away; all those dwelling in the nāga-abodes will be broken. A single pill should be placed upon the tip of a banner in the lake of the abode, and a blue flag should be fastened. Alternatively, it should be placed on the tip of a banner on a high mountain peak. At the time of a thunderbolt, the nāgas will not be able to cast down a thunderbolt. Just as the nāgas behold his golden-colored form, all the nāgas, terrified by fear, will stand still. Then it will rain as much as desired.

Oṃ suvrate vajratuṇḍe mili mili svāhā. Having fashioned an image of Āṭavaka, one should color the body of a nine-headed nāga, measuring eight finger-breadths, with vermilion (hiṅgulaka). Banners should be tied around its neck. A square mandala should be prepared and strewn with flowers. An image of the nāga should be placed in the center. An offering should be presented according to what is available.

Having consecrated a pomegranate branch twenty-one times, or one hundred and eight times, or with a thousand recitations, one should wipe the image of the nāga with that pomegranate branch. By means of the name of whichever [nāga] this is performed for, that nāga will be summoned. That nāga will no longer take pleasure in his own abode. If he does not quickly release a torrent of rain, there will be the immediate destruction of his life.

Having recited the mantra over each individual mustard seed one thousand and eight times, when the full one thousand and eight have been completed, that image of the *nāga* comes forward; it spreads its hood and acts as a serpent. Then, one should threaten it with a pomegranate vine; it becomes still and shows its tongue. It grants a vision throughout the night. All *nāgas* become subject to one's will; whatever it says, that it performs. One should consecrate milk and mustard seeds by reciting the mantra one hundred and eight times. With this, one sprinkles every location; it brings everything back under control. This is the fourth procedure.

[2.28] Then Sāgara, the great nāga king, together with other nāga kings of great supernatural power, eighty thousand nāga kings in all, rose from their seats, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, and spoke thus: "O Blessed One, most terrible mantra-words have been spoken; the ritual procedures for the accomplishment of karma are exceedingly terrible. Therefore, O Blessed One, we shall not remain steadfast in our composure for long."

We shall release showers of rain, and we shall no longer harm sentient beings. Therefore, O Blessed One, for the sake of the wicked *nāgas* and harmful *nāgas* who do not know the pledge (*samaya*), we shall recite the counteracting mantra-words. May the Blessed One empower them! O Lord of Serpents, I empower this pledge-mantra.

Homage to the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata! It is as follows: *bhuje bhuje samantabhuje tattvabhuje pravarabhuje samantākārabhuje | turu turu svāhā | samayapālane svāhā | nāgasarasaṃcodane svāhā*.

“Blessed One, this is my mantra for the *samaya* of the nāgas. It was spoken for the purpose of restraining and exhorting all wicked nāgas in the final age, in the final time. At times of excessive rain, drought, cold, heat, thunderbolts, or rain, these mantras should be remembered, so that all the nāgas will be exhorted. That *vidyādhara*, being pure and having bathed well...”

Clad in a new robe, one should go to the abode of the nāgas. In the lake of the nāga-abode, a fragrant mandala should be prepared. Having placed there an image of the Blessed One Śākyamuni or a reliquary stūpa according to what is available, it should be bathed with scented water upon that mandala. It should be worshipped with flowers, incense, and perfumes. Incense should be offered in the four directions, and all the nāgas should be invoked.

Having recited the mantra over that bathing water eighty times and having cast mustard seeds into it, one should throw it into the middle of that house. At the very moment it is thrown, that nāga-abode will roar from that water at that instant. Rising from the house in the form of smoke, a great mass of clouds appears. One should cast it into the expanse of the sky; all thunderbolts will not fall, and all winds will be bound.

All cold and unseasonable winds will subside. One should offer one thousand and eight oblations of *arkakāṣṭha* wood, ghee, mustard seeds, and *karavīra* flowers. This should be performed at a place where *nāgas* dwell, or at a well, a pond, a lotus-pool, or on a mountain peak; it succeeds everywhere. Merely by performing this rite together [with the mantra], they release great torrents of rain. During a time of excessive rain, one should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times over parched grain and mustard seeds and cast them into the air; this pacifies the excessive rain.

"O Blessed One, if we do not release a stream of rain within three nights, then, O Blessed One, may we become objects of wonder; may our bodies become utterly foul-smelling; may we become deceivers of all the Buddha-dharmas and deceivers of the three worlds; and may there be no falling away from our birth as *nāgas*. Furthermore, O Blessed One, all other rites should be performed; they are applicable in every situation."

[2.29] Then the Blessed One, having comforted the Naga king and established him in the observance (*samaya*), and having instructed the Great King Vaiśravaṇa above, departed. [2.30] The chapter titled "The Entry into the Abode of Vaiśravaṇa and the Observance of the Naga: The Release of Rain" is completed.

[3.1] Now, therefore, the Blessed One was dwelling in the Brahma-palace. Many hosts of gods had assembled; a great assembly of hosts of Bodhisattvas had gathered; and Śakra, the lord of the gods, as well as Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, the lords of the Nāgas, and those of great supernatural power—all had assembled. Also present was the Garuḍa-lord, the Great King, with golden wings, a diamond beak, and a majestic soul; his body was ablaze, he was wrathful, and possessed of terrifying prowess. He was adorned with various jewels of diverse kinds and embellished with pearls and gold.

His head was bound with a jeweled turban and he was adorned with golden ornaments. Of fierce appearance and fixed gaze, he sat upon a throne made of the king of serpents. All these arrived together with a vast retinue. And Vajrapāṇi, the lord of yakṣas, arrived accompanied by ten million yakṣas and surrounded by hundreds of thousands of vidyādharas. And Vajradhara was adorned with various jewels and gems. And the Blessed One’s body was adorned by hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of diverse rays of light.

Resplendent like a golden sacrificial pillar, shining like the sun, he bore the thirty-two major marks and the eighty minor characteristics. He was adorned with a fathom-wide aura of light; the body of the Tathāgata was perfectly pure, stainless, and luminous.

[3.2] Then the Blessed One, perceiving the great assembly gathered together, emitted from his own body a radiance of various rays. By that radiance of rays, all the ten directions were illuminated on every side.

[3.3] Then Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, and the others, having beheld the radiance of the Tathāgata, saw Jambudvīpa. Cold winds, clouds, and thunderbolts had been unleashed by wicked nāgas; all flowers, fruits, and crops, as well as the trees, grasses, shrubs, medicinal herbs, and forest giants, were scorched, destroyed, and rendered fruitless, such that Jambudvīpa was made thus.
[3.4] Then those beings, overcome by great suffering, uttered various lamentations.

[3.5] Then Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara, having prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, spoke thus: "Behold, Blessed One! Jambudvīpa has been stripped of its foliage by wicked and fierce nāgas; all have been destroyed. Sentient beings are experiencing most terrible suffering. O nāgas, this is manifest: both the fear and the miraculous empowerment of the Tathāgata. Behold the profound Buddha-knowledge, the power of the Tathāgata, and the empowerment of his extraordinary qualities."

[3.6] Then the Blessed One entered the meditative absorption called *Garuḍavijṛmbhitavilokita*, which is the miraculous manifestation of a universal garland of flames. Immediately upon his entering it, two rays of light blazed forth.
As soon as they blazed, the bodies of all the nāgas were set ablaze.
[3.7] Then the great nāga king Samantākāraparikaracchatra prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and said this: "I am burning, Blessed One! I am burning, Sugata!"

[3.8] Then the Blessed One, having consented by remaining silent, looked upward, looked all around the ten directions, and paid homage to all the Tathāgatas. Having recollected this *mahāgaruḍavegavajra*—the heart-mantra circle of the blazing splendor of Garuḍa—he uttered: *oṃ vajravati garuḍavege hūṃ hūṃ janaya visṛja hūṃ phaṭ*.

[3.9] Then those wicked nāgas arrived at that place in the expanse of the sky. The Blessed One spoke this mantra. Those wicked nāgas, having placed all their flowers, fruits, crops, leaves, and foliage before the Blessed One, stood before him in a state of humiliation, trembling violently. [3.10] Then the Blessed Tathāgata uttered the Great Heart-mantra named Garuḍajvālā.

Homage to the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata! Oṃ jvala jvala! Prajvala prajvala! Hana hana! O you who rend the hearts of all nāgas! Hana hana the strength, vigor, and prowess of all nāgas! Daha daha the bodies of all nāgas! Paca paca the vital points (*marmāṇi*) of all nāgas! With the flapping of the wings of Garuḍa, fly, fly down upon the abodes of all nāgas! Oṃ matha matha, you who wear the great wish-fulfilling jewel on your crown, you who wear the great attire of Garuḍa!
