[3.11] This, O Lord of Serpents, is the Great Heart Dhāraṇī called the Garuḍa Flame of the Tathāgata’s Pledge; it is for the restraint of all wicked nāgas, the destruction and warding off of all clouds, thunderbolts, and wind-storms, and the protection of the crops.

The protection of flowers, fruits, and trees, the production of ambrosial fruit, and the increase of happiness and prosperity—by the mere act of reciting this [mantra] of the Lord of Serpents, this entire circle of nāgas, together with their sons, wives, chief ministers, and retinues, including the venomous *sītavalāhaka* and *vāyuvalāhaka* nāgas, shall, by the power of their collective presence, be authorized by the word of the Tathāgata.

By the empowerment of the Tathāgata’s samaya, in this Jambudvīpa, during the final age and the final time, all crops, all flowers and fruits, and all substances such as grasses and medicinal herbs must be protected and preserved. †In no other way†, you must release showers of rain from time to time. Just as [you preserve] your own life, so must you preserve the great flowers, fruits, and crops of those in Jambudvīpa. All this shall come to pass exactly as it is, by the authorization of the Tathāgata.

If one should transgress through the gravity of his word, then may all the abodes of the nāgas be set ablaze, thoroughly inflamed, and become a single mass of flame. May a great famine of nāgas manifest; may they become devoid of strength and have their vigor destroyed. May they be deprived of water, and may there be a drying up of their dwellings. May their bodies become coarse, and may they be constantly terrified by fire and sand, as well as by hunger and thirst.

Running hither and thither, their radiance scorched away, tormented by the heat of the sun, may they be burned by his burning body. You shall be seized by various diseases, calamities, and afflictions. Thus, in the final age, in the final time, wicked *nāgas* who are fierce and malevolent will experience suffering if they transgress this *dhāraṇī* called the "Tathāgata-Garuḍa-Flame-Heart. Therefore, then—
O Lord of Serpents, you must remain true to your vow and protect the commitment of the Tathāgata. All sentient beings of Jambudvīpa must be protected, guarded, and brought to fulfillment.

[3.12] Then there were the great nāga kings Samantākāraparikaracchatra, Sāgara, the nāga kings Nanda and Upananda, the nāga king Manasvī, the nāga king Huluṇḍa, Varuṇa, Ratnajvālāsaṃdhāraṇavikasitaprakarṣaṇacūḍa, Brahmaśīrṣa, Trailokyavikhyātadhvaja, Īśvaraprabha, Viśuddhaprabhāsakīrti, and Samantākāradhvaja.

And Maṇiśīrṣa; and Supratiṣṭhitabrahmacūḍa; and Jvalitacūḍāvali; and Mahāsamudrākramaṇa; and Samantāvalokitanetra; and Viṣṇucakravartin, the great nāga king; and Sumerudhvaja; and Samantākāravigata; and Praharṣitavarṣaṇa; and Prasphoṭana; and Vidyujjvālī; and Airāvaṇa, the great nāga king; and Jalavāhanacitra; and Mucilindabala; and Trailokyavarṣaṇa.
The great nāga king Vaiśravaṇacitra was at the head of these eighty-four thousand nāga kings; each of these nāga kings [was accompanied] by seventy-seven [thousand].

Surrounded by thousands of nāga families from that abode, she approached the Blessed One; having approached, she circumambulated the Blessed One three times, honored him with great worship, prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, and addressed the Blessed One as follows: "We are ruined, O Blessed One! We are consumed, our bodies set ablaze. Our hair stands on end with terror. O Blessed One, most dreadful mantra-words have been spoken—words that are exceedingly fierce and difficult to withstand."

Blessed One, when we were all standing before the Blessed One in person, we were thus terrified and trembling, our hair standing on end with agitation, overwhelmed by a great and most dreadful fear; we all remained there with our minds deeply disturbed. Therefore, Blessed One, how will the monks be in the future time, in the final age, after the Tathāgata has passed into parinirvāṇa? They will become fierce, driven by greed for gain, intent only on warding off cold, wind, and lightning.
Therefore, Blessed One, how should one deal with those wicked nāgas? How will they restore their lives? And how, Blessed One, will our sons and grandsons experience [the consequences]?

[3.13] Then the Blessed One said this to those lords of the *nāgas*: "O lords of the serpents, you must dwell in loving-kindness during the final age, in the final time. You must act in accordance with the Tathāgata’s covenant. From time to time, release showers of rain; from time to time, bring forth flowers, fruits, and crops; and [ward off] all winds, clouds, and thunderbolts."

"Restrain yourselves! Do not destroy them! Then, O lords of serpents, you shall dwell free from affliction in the future time, in the final age. "If, O lords of serpents, you do not properly observe this covenant, then I shall not be at fault, O lords of serpents. This is the first mantra for the exhortation of those who have committed no offense.

[3.15] Now, therefore, I shall proclaim the ritual procedure for the Root-Vidyā, which is esteemed by the minds of the *nāgas*. Having recited this *Jvalitagaruḍatejohṛdayadhāraṇī*, one should first gaze into the sky and scatter a mixture of mustard seeds and parched grain in the four directions. All clouds and thunderbolts will be paralyzed; all *nāgas* will remain trembling. Having recited it twenty-one times over ashes and water, one should sprinkle them to perform self-protection.

It shall come to pass: having consecrated one hundred and eight mustard seeds with the mantra, and having consecrated water seven times at the time of a thundercloud’s roar, one should then throw a mustard seed into the sky; it will cause a binding of the clouds in the sky. All flowers and fruits taken toward the clouds will fall to the ground. The mantra should be recollected. If one is angry, the syllable *phaṭ* should be uttered. By three utterances of *phaṭ*, the nāgas fall face-downward; even the bodies of the nāgas shatter and fall upon the dry land.

Having recited [the mantra] over a pomegranate branch twenty-one times, one should whirl it seven times in a circular motion. All wicked *nāgas*, cold winds, clouds, and thunderbolts fall upon the earth; their heads split into seven pieces, and their eyes burst open. By whirling it with anger one hundred and eight times, all the neighboring clouds and *nāgas* together with their retinues fall to the ground.

The entire abode of the nāgas, including its waters, trees, forests, and shrubs, becomes a single mass of flame. And all the great nāga kings, possessing great majesty and great supernatural power (*maharddhika*), become seized by a severe headache. If the *vidyādhara* quickly recites the mantra, there shall be a total derangement of their families; they, along with their sons, grandsons, retinues, and mounts, shall perish and go to destruction. At a time of drought, one should take mustard seeds, recite the mantra over them a thousand times, and scatter them within the abode.

And all the nāgas tremble violently; their palaces and lakes will become a single mass of flame. They quickly discharge torrents of rain, and again and again they discharge torrents of rain according to their desire.

When it is time for rain, the Vidyādhara should recite the mantra one hundred and eight times over mustard seeds and water. Having ascended to a high place and stood facing the east, he should cast seven handfuls of water toward the eastern direction while reciting the mantra seven times; immediately all the Nāga kings will assemble together in the midst [of the rain] and release torrents of rain.

At dawn, having recited the mantra seven times over water mixed with mustard seeds and saffron, it should be sprinkled in the four directions; it should also be sprinkled below and above. A boundary will be established for one *yojana* in every direction against all cold winds, clouds, and thunderbolts, and all malevolent *nāgas* will be bound.

They shall come to be; all the nāgas shall become impossible to overcome. Taking fresh cow dung from a tawny cow that has not fallen [to the ground], one should take its ghee, milk, and urine, along with the seven kinds of seeds, and mix them together. Having recited the mantra over this ninety times, one should then fashion a five-headed nāga. With its hood-jewels displayed, sitting in the cross-legged posture, and turned around, it should be smeared with white sandalwood and saffron and placed upon a pure seat. A silk-cloth consecration (paṭṭābhiṣeka) should be performed.

A garland of flowers should be offered. Seven vessels made of *rasika* wood, shaped like jars, should be set out. Curd, milk, rice, sugarcane juice, sugar, honey, fruits, and flowers should be poured into those very vessels. A square mandala should be prepared. It should be strewn with flowers. Four full jars should be set out. Four arrows should be planted. Four white banners should be fastened. An offering (*bali*) should be placed in the central mandala.

Four stakes of *khadira* wood should be driven into the four corners of the mandala. It should be encircled with a five-colored thread consisting of five strands. In every instance, the rite should be performed after reciting the mantra twenty-one times. A bell should be tied to the top of the water-jar (*kumbha*). *Nalada*, resin of *sarja*, *kunduruka*, *nakha*, *nāgapuṣpa*, white mustard seeds, and sugar should be mixed together; this should be done while the mantra has been recited one hundred and eight times.
Incense should be offered by him. This incense is to be employed everywhere. Then the vidyādhara must be well-bathed and wear clean garments; [he should act] with this very mantra.

One should perform the ritual sipping of water (*upaspṛśana*), the binding of the topknot (*śikhābandha*), the binding of the boundary (*sīmābandha*), the binding of the mandala (*maṇḍalabandhana*), the raising of the garment (*vastrotkṣepana*), self-protection (*ātmarakṣā*), and the bath (*snāna*). Having placed the Nāga facing east, the Vidyādhara should sit facing him and perform the invocation (*āvāhana*), the offering of food (*bali*), flowers, and incense, as well as the dismissal (*visarjana*), all with that very mantra. Then the Vidyādhara should recite the mantra one thousand and eight times. Having consecrated each mustard seed or fruit with the mantra, they should be struck against the image of the Nāga. Four lamps of clarified butter (*ghṛtapradīpa*) should be offered.

The *nāgas* should be invoked. He who performs the invocation shall receive their presence. When the recitation of one thousand and eight mantras is completed, all the great *nāga* kings become subject to his will. They will grant him a vision at all times and provide everything according to his desires. They will explain everything in detail. Together with all their kinsmen, retinues, sons, and grandsons, they become subject to him;
they perform all tasks and protect him as if he were their own home.

[3.16] An image of a *nāga* maiden should be placed in a secret location. Flowers and incense should be offered. It should be kept in a secluded place; it must not be revealed or shown to anyone. It should be covered with a clean cloth. When a task is to be performed, one should strike it with mustard seeds over which the mantra has been recited eight hundred times. It will accomplish all tasks. Wherever one sends it, there it goes; it returns again. It tells everything in a dream.

He will become a performer of all tasks according to the purpose required; he is called the "Commander of Nāgas. Whenever untimely clouds, winds, lightning, and frost shall arise, then one should [use] fierce seeds mixed with mustard.

Having recited [the mantra] one hundred and one times, one should angrily strike the form of the nāga; at that very moment, all winds and thunderbolts will perish, and all [obstructing spirits] will be bound. During a time of drought, having written the mantra on a strip of cloth (*cīrikā*), wrapped it with red thread, and tied twenty-one knots, one should bind it around the neck of a nāga image. One should then recite [the mantra] over the head of the nāga twenty-one times. At that very moment, they will release torrents of rain, raining as much as desired.

During a time of excessive rain, one should recite the *nīlasūtraka* seven times and tie seven knots; the excessive rain will then subside. Furthermore, there are other methods for the accomplishment of ritual sciences (*kalpavidyā*) in all cases. This is the aforementioned mantra; it should be recalled seven times beforehand. It is employed everywhere; by merely reciting it, accomplishment is achieved in all instances.
[3.17] The *Dhāraṇī* named "The Circle of the Heart of Garuḍa Blazing with the Great Speed of Garuḍa and Vajra-Speed" is completed.

[4.1] Now, therefore, shall follow the ritual procedure for the service of the Root Heart-mantra. Merely by its being uttered, all the *nāgas* tremble violently. To ward off wind and clouds, one should hold a pomegranate creeper or a *karavīra* creeper over a high lake. One should prepare a circular mandala out of fallen cow dung, square and well-proportioned according to its own dimensions. One should drive eight stakes of *khadira* wood, each measuring eight finger-breadths in length; one should drive them into the ten directions and the four corners.

One should bury five arrows and a trident. The four arrows are to be wrapped all around with a five-colored thread. Four full jars, four incense burners, and exactly four offering jars should be placed. A jar filled with white offerings should be placed in the central mandala. One should cause it to be strewn with flowers and scatter parched grain and mustard seeds. Having recited the mantra over each of these seven times, they should be buried.

One should bind the boundary in the four directions with mustard seeds and water over which the mantra has been recited. This becomes a great binding of the boundary. For a distance of one *yojana* all around, wicked *nāgas* will not be able to descend there. Likewise, even great *nāgas* will never be able to bring down untimely cold winds, clouds, or lightning; nor will they be able to cause harm, not even a blade of grass or a leaf. All shall be bound, afflicted by the fivefold bonds.

In this way, the boundary-binding shall remain for eight months. Neither yakṣas, nor bhūtas, nor rākṣasas, nor pretas, kumbhāṇḍas, or guhyakas can transgress this established limit. Then, the vidyādhara, standing in the center of the maṇḍala, should ward off the nāgas with a pomegranate branch over which the mantra has been recited seven times. One should not ward them off too harshly. The nāga-paryaṅka mudrā should be bound: the index fingers should be made into the hood of a serpent, while the little fingers should be extended.

This mudrā of all the nāgas, by its mere commencement, will cause all the nāgas to be afflicted; headaches and migraines will manifest. If the nāgas desire to destroy that place, heated sand will fall upon their heads, as many times as there are heads, tails, and trunks; for that many showers of sword-blades will fall upon their bodies. Thereupon, all the nāgas will dwell in fear and trembling.

Then, in Jambudvīpa, they release showers of rain from time to time; all wicked nāgas become submissive. Having recited the mantra twenty-one times over a stake of khadira wood, one should offer incense upon a square mandala strewn with flowers at a lake situated on high ground.

Having offered as a sacrificial oblation (*bali*) a vessel full of mustard-seed water over which the mantra has been recited seven times, one should drive a stake of *khadira* wood into the center of the mandala. All faults caused by wind, clouds, lightning, and cold will be bound; all shall become paralyzed. As long as the stake is not pulled out, they remain bound. Having consecrated a mustard seed with the mantra seven times, it should be thrown toward the cloud; all lightning bolts will turn into water.

Having recited the mantra twenty-one times over a *karavīra* creeper, it should be used as a girdle; in all cases, one will be bound by lightning. One should throw water consecrated seven times [into the fire]; one becomes released. Having recited the mantra twenty-one times over a trident, it should be driven into the ground in the midst of thundering clouds; as long as the trident is not pulled out, there will be a binding of the thundering clouds. Upon its being pulled out, there is release.

Having recited the mantra over a sword seven times and having assumed the nāgaparyaṅka mudrā, one should stand facing the clouds. As soon as it is grasped, it will burst into flames. All the nāgas will be terrified. Having taken the sword and recited the mantra one hundred and eight times, one should draw a garuḍa upon it with saffron and then cause it to terrify [the nāgas]. To the extent that one causes the sword to terrify them, to that same extent the garuḍa’s wings will fall upon their bodies. All the nāgas will be terrified and flee in the ten directions.

Furthermore, they will no longer be able to hurl thunderbolts. One should offer sixty oblations of *karavīra* flowers mixed with ghee and mustard seeds into a circular mandala for one year; then all the *nāgas*, the cool-clouds, the thunderbolts, and even the snow and so forth, will be paralyzed. When it is time for rain, they will pour down water. One should fashion a three-headed *nāga* out of beeswax measuring four finger-breadths in height, and scatter parched grain and mustard seeds [upon it].

It should be covered with gold; having placed a white cloth over it, one should recite the mantra one thousand times. Taking a new clay pot that has not been touched, it should be placed in the center of that [area], and then covered with a head-cloth.

It should be sealed. A water jar should be placed there, and a square maṇḍala made of cow dung should be prepared. Puffed rice and mustard seeds should be scattered over it. Incense should be offered. Having placed the jar there, the mantra should be recited. After chanting the mantra seven times over a pomegranate creeper, one should strike the jar very gently with that very creeper. All thunderbolts will enter into the middle of the jar, and all nāgas will become subject to one's control.

And that nāga is made of beeswax, upon which the name of the nāga-king should be inscribed. By means of whose name one recites the vidyā, that nāga appears before them together with his retinue. Then, appearing in the form of a brahmin, he performs everything that one commands.

[4.2] Having gone above the nāga-abode of that unrighteous nāga king—who fails to protect his realm and destroys the crops, flowers, and fruits—one who is well-bathed and wearing clean garments should recite the vidyā twenty-one times. Then, from the nāga-abode, very elderly women emerge and say: "What will you do, O vidyādhara?"

One must not speak. The ground should be struck with a *vajra* and the syllable *phaṭ* should be uttered. Then that Vṛddhikā, being urged by her desire, says: "I am dying! I am dying! and they enter the palace. The inhabitants of the palace ask: "Why have you come? A cruel *vidyādhara* stands at the door of the palace. Then the *nāga*, his body trembling with fear, assumes the form of a young boy and stands before the *vidyādhara*. He asks: "O *vidyādhara*, what will you do?"

The Vidyādhara should first recite the previous mantra. With a pomegranate branch, he should angrily strike the ground. [The Nāga] will say, "O Vidyādhara, what shall I do at every command? Then the Vidyādhara should say, "Observe the commitments (*samaya*) of the Tathāgata. [The Nāga] will say, "I shall observe them all. The Vidyādhara will say, "Nāga, take up the ten wholesome actions (*daśakuśala*). [The Nāga] will say, "I take them up, O Vidyādhara. [The Vidyādhara] will say, "Nāga, accept the three refuges (*triśaraṇa*)."

"I grant you favor, O Vidyādhara! Extract the kīla! It must not be extracted! Thus one should say: "Grant me the training in the Tathāgata’s samaya. Then I extract the kīla from the kīla. Thereupon that nāga, together with his retinue, falls at [the practitioner's] feet. One should cause him to recollect the taking of the three refuges and the ten paths of virtuous action, which are to be bestowed; he is to be made to accept the samayas.

Then the stake should be extracted; one should take food at that very spot. All the nāgas become subject to one's will. They perform whatever tasks are desired, dwelling [there] as if in their own home. They will carry out all duties and obey commands. Wherever one sends them, they go there and shall perform every task. Furthermore, no wicked nāgas will remain in that nāga family. From time to time they release showers of rain;
from time to time they bring forth crops, including leaves, flowers, fruits, and foliage.

They bring about [the desired results], and they shall no longer cause harm. This great dhāraṇī is accomplished through mere recitation; it should be employed in all rites, for there is the accomplishment of all rites—the supreme, unsurpassed accomplishment.
[4.3] The ritual procedure for the root mantra, along with its ancillary practices, is completed.

[5.1] Then the King of Garuḍas, having bowed with palms joined toward where the Blessed One was, addressed the Blessed One as follows: "Blessed One, for the sake of all sentient beings and for the fulfillment of all their hopes, I shall proclaim the dhāraṇī named Vajratuṇḍajvālavidyut, which inflames the hearts of all nāgas, wards off all untimely winds, clouds, and thunderbolts, brings forth all flowers and fruits, and increases all the essential juices of the earth. May the Blessed One grant his empowerment for this.

[5.2] Then the Blessed One said this to the Great Lord of Garuḍas: "O Lord of Great Garuḍas, I have empowered this dhāraṇī named Vajratuṇḍā, which has been empowered by hundreds of thousands of millions of Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksambuddhas, as numerous as the sands of the river Gaṅgā. Speak it, O Lord of Garuḍas, for the sake of subduing wicked nāgas.
[5.3] Then the King of Garuḍas spoke this dhāraṇī named Vajratuṇḍā.

Homage to the Three Jewels! Homage to Caṇḍavajrapāṇi, the great general of the yakṣas! Homage to the Lord of the Three Worlds! Homage to the Four Great Kings! Oṃ vajratuṇḍe! Tuṇḍe tuṇḍe! Mahātuṇḍe! Tuṭi tuṭi! Vajraśikharatuṇḍe! O you whose body is adorned with various ornaments of jewels and gold! Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ!

The Heart-Mantra for Driving Away the Naga Kings: Sphoṭaya vajratuṇḍena svāhā! Sarvākālameghāśaniṃ nivāraya hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ svāhā! Mahāvajrajvālāya svāhā! Sarvaduṣṭanāgavināśanāya svāhā! Garuḍahṛdayāya svāhā! Garuḍatuṇḍāya svāhā! Suvarṇapakṣanipātanāya svāhā! Oṃ dhuru dhuru svāhā! Muru muru svāhā!
Svāhā! Turu turu svāhā! Ruṭ ruṭ ruṭ ruṭ ruṭ || 5 || Hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ hūṃ || 10 || Phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ || 5 || Svāhā!

[5.4] As soon as this Vajratuṇḍa-dhāraṇī was spoken by Garuḍa, eight million billion trillion great nāga kings fell face-down; their limbs were perspiring, their bodies were set ablaze, and they fainted, rolling upon the surface of the earth, as they all uttered these most dreadful words of the great dhāraṇī mantras.

With their bodies trembling, they prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One and spoke thus: "May the Blessed One protect us! May the Sugata protect us! O Blessed One, we shall no longer destroy Jambudvīpa; we shall no longer destroy the flowers, fruits, and crops. We shall maintain, O Blessed One, that this spot of earth is to be treated as a shrine (caitya). Wherever this Great King of Kalpas shall circulate, there this Vajratuṇḍā Dhāraṇī shall circulate."

In that regard, Blessed One, we shall always and constantly maintain [this] as equal to a Tathāgata shrine. We shall always and constantly provide protection, defense, and guardianship in that location—whether in a city, a district, a marketplace, a forest hermitage, a village, a house, or a monastery.

We shall ward off all cold winds, thunderbolts, and unseasonable clouds. We shall produce smooth-bodied, pleasing, fragrant, abundant, and potent juices, as well as all flowers, fruits, and crops. We shall pacify all strife, impurities, famine, harsh speech, and ill omens. From time to time we shall release showers of rain, and we shall bring forth both grain and the fruits of flowering plants. [We shall likewise ward off] all gadflies, mosquitoes, locusts, and reptiles...

We shall ward off even frogs, *tryambukas*, flies, *trailāṭakas*, centipedes, bees, parrots, and mynas; we shall destroy them. We shall pacify all calamities. And, O Blessed One, we shall no longer conduct ourselves with the practice of evil dharmas. We shall cause all droughts and lack of rain to disappear. O Blessed One, we shall remain firm by means of our oath and vow. O Blessed One, we shall constantly observe the training and restraint of the Three Jewels.
"Furthermore, Blessed One, we shall no longer cause harm to the beings of Jambudvīpa;

rather, we shall protect them as if they were our own children. Blessed One, authorized by the words of the Tathāgata, in the future time, in the final age, we shall protect all beings, we shall sustain them, and we shall bring about their well-being, security, and abundance.
Then the Blessed One, having comforted those dragon kings, said this: "O lords of serpents, you shall do so. Do not be indifferent!"
[5.6] Now we shall explain the procedure for the ritual service (*upacāra*).
It is auspicious and performs all rites.
This mantra, the Sole Hero (*ekavīra*), will accomplish every purpose.

The wise and learned one should cause it to be remembered once, in a high place, with a loud voice and sound; wherever that sound is heard, at all times, cold winds, clouds, thunderbolts, and lightning shall not overcome that place. Furthermore, it is impossible for anyone to steal its vital energy (*ojas*) or to harm it. The Vidyādhara should stand facing east in a high place—on a mountain, in a forest hermitage, a village, or a monastery—whichever location is most elevated.

One who is pure, wearing clean garments and white clothes, should prepare a square mandala smeared with clay and cow dung. A heap of arrows measuring one cubit (hasta) should be placed in the center of the mandala. The mantra should be recited twenty-one times. Khadira wood stakes, each eight finger-breadths in length, should be driven into the four corners of the mandala; having consecrated them twenty-one times with the mantra, they should be encircled on all sides with a five-colored thread tripled in thickness.

Having consecrated a small incense burner seven times, one should fumigate the maṇḍala. Mustard seeds should be scattered; having consecrated them twenty-one times, flowers should also be strewn about. Four circles of jars should be placed. One should set out an offering (bali) in the center of the maṇḍala facing the four directions. It should consist of curd, milk, sugar, rice, molasses, and all [other ingredients] combined. A boundary-binding (sīmābandha) should be established in the four directions. And parched grain and mustard seeds should have the mantra recited over them five times.

It should be performed on the full moon of the fifteenth day. It should be recited in a loud voice. Mustard seeds should be scattered in the four directions, below, and above. One should cause all the nāgas to be expelled during their respective days. As soon as this ritual procedure is performed, all untimely clouds, thunderbolts, and wicked nāgas will be bound; they will be paralyzed.

All ill omens, calamities, misfortunes, afflictions, and the seizing spirits, ghosts, piśācas, yakṣas, and rākṣasas will avoid them from afar. A boundary-binding extends for a hundred yojanas in every direction. All diseases, all ailments, and all those with malicious intent—whether adversaries or enemies—will have no power over them. All flowers, fruits, and crops will become perfectly developed; they will be fully ripened and delicious in flavor.

All seeds, when well-nourished, will sprout and grow. All malevolent rites, sorcery, and *kākhorda* spells will perish. As long as [the image] is not removed, the boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) will remain established. For that long, all the *nāgas* will release showers of rain at the proper times. All flowers, fruits, and crops will grow in full abundance. Wherever there is a task, it shall be accomplished if one recollects [this practice] even once; it succeeds. One should fashion a *garuḍa* out of beeswax, measuring eight finger-breadths, seated in the cross-legged posture with wings spread wide.

The seat is that of a Nāga king. He has nine heads, with serpents bound upon his crown. With his right hand he holds a three-headed [serpent], and with his left hand he holds a jewel-gem; one should cover him with glowing gold. One should touch him with colored powders according to the ritual procedure. He should be placed atop a variegated cloth for a day and night, and the mantra should be recited one thousand times. Even if there is no physical strength, one should eat white food. Furthermore, one must bathe; thus it is to be accomplished.

Guggulu incense should be offered. Flowers, incense, and sacrificial offerings should be presented according to one's means. A lamp should be lit and placed directly in front of it. It will grant a vision; it will speak and bestow all boons; it performs every rite; and it carries out whatever command is given. It should be maintained in a secluded, secret place. When there is a time of drought, the Vidyādhara should take it and lead it to the abode of the Nāgas.

Having placed [the vessel] in the lake of the nāga-abode and offered incense, one should scatter mustard seeds into the middle of the abode while reciting the mantra three times. Immediately, all the nāgas will release a torrent of rain. If they do not rain immediately, then they will see the nāga-abode filled on all sides with garuḍas; it will become a single mass of flames, heated sand will fall upon their heads, and the water will dry up.

In the event of excessive rain, one should show it facing the clouds, and the rain will cease. In all cases, it should be displayed toward the winds, thunderbolts, cold, rain, and clouds; in an instant, [the calamity] ceases. Within a radius of seven and a half *yojanas* in all four directions, thunderbolts do not fall, nor will the winds of the cold season prevail again; they all become paralyzed. During a disturbance of the winds, it should be placed at crossroads.

Alternatively, at the city gate, all winds will be paralyzed in an instant; even the Vairambha wind will be paralyzed and bound, and it will not be possible to set it in motion again. At the mere sight of him, all *nāgas* will flee.
[5.7] The *dhāraṇī* named *Sarvagaruḍahṛdayapaṭhitasiddhaparamasiddhavajratuṇḍā* is completed.

[6.1] Then Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, and the four Great Kings approached the Blessed One; having approached and circumambulated the Blessed One three times, they said this to the Blessed One: "O Blessed One, we too, all gathered together, shall proclaim the dhāraṇī named *Jvalitavajrāśanituṇḍā* (The Blazing Thunderbolt-Beak)."

"We shall bestow that which captivates the hearts of all nāgas, withers their hearts, destroys the families of wicked nāgas, wards off all winds, clouds, and thunderbolts, and brings to fruition all crops, flowers, and fruits. May the Blessed One empower it for the benefit of all sentient beings.

[6.2] Then the Blessed One spoke thus to Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, and the four Great Kings: "Speak, noble sons! It has been empowered by me for the benefit, welfare, and happiness of all sentient beings."

[6.3] Then Brahmā, Viṣṇu, Maheśvara, and the four Great Kings spoke this dhāraṇī: Homage to the Triple Gem! Homage to the Blessed One, Śākyamuni, the Tathāgata, the Arhat, the Samyaksambuddha! Homage to Caṇḍavajrapāṇi! Homage to the Holder of the Fierce Vajra, possessed of great strength and prowess! Homage to the Embodiment of the Three Worlds! Homage to the Four Great Kings! Homage to the one with the fierce, loud laughter blazing like a vajra-thunderbolt! *Matha matha pramatha!* (Churn, churn, subdue!)

Pramatha! O you of blazing and distorted face! Victory, victory! O you of great strength, heroism, and prowess! O King of Wrath! O Brahmā! O Subrahmā! O you of Brahma-voice! Ho, ho, Lord of Nāgas! Disperse, disperse! Otherwise, we shall split your head with the Brahma-staff—*hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ*! *Bhara bhara*, you who hold the discus of Viṣṇu in your hand! O Lord of Serpents, do not transgress! Otherwise, I shall cut off your head with the discus of Viṣṇu!

Bhūṭali bhūṭali bhūṭali bhūṭali bhūṭali || 5 || Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Let all the wicked nāgas faint, faint, faint! Shatter their hearts! O wielder of the blazing trident of Maheśvara, slay, slay, hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ! Muci muci! Tuṭi tuṭi! Bhara bhara! Kṣaṇi, O you who possess the blazing spear of the four Great Kings! Dhara dhara, hūṃ phaṭ!

Flash! Flash! Quiver! Quiver! Move! Move! Destroy the hearts of the wicked *nāgas*! Burst asunder! *Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ!* Withdraw! Withdraw! Reduce to ashes the wicked thunderbolt-wind-clouds, the cold winds, and the flames of lightning! *Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!* Remember your vow! O Lord of Serpents! O You who possess the form of Viṣṇu! O you, *tuṭi tuṭi*! *Hūṃ hūṃ phaṭ phaṭ svāhā!* For the destruction of the thunderbolt, *hūṃ phaṭ svāhā!*

The heart-mantras of all the nāgas for the bursting [of obstacles]: *sphoṭakāya hūṃ phaṭ svāhā*. To the one beheld by the Buddhas, *svāhā*. To Brahmā, *svāhā*. To the form of Viṣṇu, *svāhā*. To Maheśvara with his blazing trident, *svāhā*.

To the upholder of the pledge of the Four Great Kings, *svāhā*. To the serpent, *svāhā*. To the lord of serpents, *svāhā*. Oṃ *dhiri dhiri svāhā*. To the blazing vajra, *svāhā*. To the one who causes the hair to stand on end, *svāhā*. *stuṭi suṭi putreṭi svāhā*. *phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ phaṭ*. 5.

[6.4] Immediately upon the recitation of the *dhāraṇī* named *Jvalitavajrāśanituṇḍā*, all the wicked *nāgas* stood there with their bodies wet and foul-smelling, their variegated bodies becoming limp and slack. Prostrating at the feet of the Blessed One, they spoke thus: "May the Blessed One protect us, for we are loathsome! We have been ruined, O Blessed One, by the world including the gods. O Blessed One, henceforth we shall no longer harass the beings in Jambudvīpa, nor shall we harm them, even in the slightest degree."
"We shall not even look upon him, much less allow him entry.

[6.5] Now, if one performs this ritual service, by the mere act of remembering it, the bodies of all the *nāgas* will be shattered into pieces; their bodies will become moist, foul-smelling, and putrid. Having consecrated a mustard seed twenty-one times with mantras, it should be thrown in the four directions; all the *nāgas* will be bound. A boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) extending seven *yojanas* in every direction will be established. Having consecrated a vajra one hundred and eight times, the *nāgas* should be warded off.

By being reminded of it even once, all winds, clouds, and thunderbolts will be warded off; they will all perish. By merely remembering it a thousand times, all thunderbolts will perish in an instant. If there is a thunderbolt of adamant (vajrāśani), it will cause water to flow forth within a mere moment. At the time of a thunderbolt, one should whirl the vajra in whichever direction [the danger arises].

The thunderbolt whirls there in every direction and causes it to move; all thunderbolts fall down. At dawn, having gone to a secluded place and being in solitary retreat, one should bind the paryaṅka mudrā and recite this mantra thirty-two times. As soon as it is set in motion, all wind-clouds and thunderbolts are destroyed; all wicked nāgas are destroyed and no longer have power. [One should scatter] mustard seeds in the four directions.

It should be thrown [into the water]. A boundary-binding (*sīmābandha*) is established for one year. All winds, clouds, and thunderbolts will be bound; all *nāgas* will become submissive. Together with their sons, grandsons, and retinues, they will be constantly and perpetually bound [to service]. They will perform every task. Having recited [the mantra] twenty-one times over a jar, it should be given at the time of a thunderbolt; the heads of all wicked *nāgas* will burst open, and the sky will become the surface of the earth. This *dhāraṇī* is everywhere unimpeded.

[6.6] Then the Blessed One granted his approval to Mahāgaruḍendra, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Maheśvara: "Excellent, excellent, Great Brahmā! Well-spoken are these words uttered; this great vidyā, this dhāraṇī-mantra phrase, has been established in Jambudvīpa for the sake of the welfare and happiness of all sentient beings, for the purpose of subduing wicked nāgas who are merciless, pitiless, and harmful, for the purpose of restraining them, and for the purpose of inflicting punishment upon others. [6.7] Then Sāgara, the king of the nāgas, together with the kings of the nāgas headed by Samantākāraparikara and Chatrākara—

Accompanied by the great nāga kings Atiprema, Taijaska, Maharddhika, and Mahānāga, as well as hundreds of thousands of millions of billions of other wicked nāgas, he approached the Blessed One. Having approached, he bowed his head at the feet of the Blessed One and addressed him thus: "Blessed One, a great assembly of nāgas has gathered. Together with our assembly and our retinues, we shall all, through our collective power, [protect] all the beings of Jambudvīpa in the future time, in the final age."

We shall protect all flowers, fruits, crops, leaves, and foliage; we shall ward off all winds, thunderbolts, cold, and heat; from time to time we shall release showers of rain; we shall cause grasses, shrubs, medicinal herbs, and crops to grow; by our own oaths and promises, we shall observe the covenant of the Tathāgata; we shall fulfill the hopes and desires of all sentient beings; and we shall not cause them harm.

“O Blessed One, if this King of Rituals, the mantra-dhāraṇī, should exceed the aforementioned specific qualities, may we not attain perfect awakening; this is our oath. It is as follows: Oṃ ṭaki caki guli gumuli sasa gugu ṭiṭi viriṭi huyu huhu riṭi svāhā.”

"O Blessed One, this is the Naga-pledge. In the future time, in the final age, when there are wicked *nāgas*, lightning, excessive rain, unseasonable rain, wind, clouds, thunderbolts, cold winds, and the falling of lightning at improper times—a *vidyādhara* should recite this pledge seven times with a loud voice, facing eastward, either in a high refuge or on a mountain. Having consecrated mustard seeds with the mantra, they should be scattered in the four directions. As soon as they are scattered and merely uttered, the bodies of all the *nāgas* shall shatter into a hundred pieces."
They would destroy them; they do not remain, but rather hiss. Then they quickly release showers of rain.
"Thus it was said by the Blessed One: 'O Lord of Serpents, this should be maintained as a dhāraṇī.
[6.8] The Noble Vajratuṇḍa, the King of Ritual Manuals concerning the Samaya, is completed.
